Outline and Justifications for Chapter Four: Experiments and Evaluation

Title: Chapter Four: Experiments and Evaluation

4.1 Overview and Objectives
- Explain the exact purpose of the experiments chapter 
- Describe how this chapter makes the methodology from chapter 3 function and measure the evaluation
- Clarify that this chapter evaluates the behavior of the system rather than predictive performance
- Provide a high level summary of: 
a. design framework
b. Evaluation metrics and thresholds
c. Stats and analysis methods 
d. Responsible computing validation 
- Establish the overall goal:
- Determine weather CaddySense behaves consistently, transparently, and responsibly under controlled testing conditions.
- Clarifies scope boundaries: 
a. No predictive modeling accuracy claims 
b. No human tampering trials
c. Evaluations is system-centered rather than outcome-centered

4.2 Experimental Design Framework

4.2.1 Research questions
- Define the core research questions guiding evaluation
a. Does the rule-based analytics layer able to produce deterministic and reproducible classification?
b. Does the conversational AI support its feedback in measurable metrics?
c. Does the system adhere to predefined restrictions (practice time limits, output length)
d. Does the advice appropriately adapt to different golfer skill tiers? 
e. Does the system maintain clear when data is incomplete or vague?
Explain how the research question maps and how it directly points to a measurable validation strategy

4.2.2 Experimental Environment and Output context
- A description of evaluation environment:
a. Local execution (non-cloud)
b. Consumer level Hardware
c. Offline inference 
- Rationale: 
a. Ensures privacy 
b. Maintains reproducibility 
c. Controls external variability
- Justify why the evaluation did not involve real time sensor feeds
- Explain controlled testing conditions 
(Figure: 4.1. Experimental execution environment overview)

4.2.3 Synthetic Golfer Profile Construction 
- Tell of how test cases were designed 
- Justify for synthetic data rather than real user Data
- Profile categories: 
a. Beginner (High handicap, low GIR, inconsistent putting)
b. Intermediate (moderate consistency, mixed strengths)
c. Advanced recreational (low handicap, marginal inefficiencies)
d. Distance-dominant but inaccurate
e. High varied profile
f. Missing-data profile
g. Extreme, but valid metric profile
- Explain:
a. Controlled variable isolation
b. Reproducibility logic
c. Internal validity benefits 
(Table 4.1 synthetic golfer test profiles and characteristics)

4.6 Threats to Validity

4.6.1 Internal Validity Threats 
- Synthetic data limits
- Evaluate the subjectivity in the scoring 
- Control the testing environment

4.6.2 External Validity Threats
- Limited to recreational golfers
- no Real world testing
- Hardware restrictions

4.6.3 Build Validity Threats
- The partial reliance on assessment 
- No outside coaching expert benchmark
- Metric-grounding measurement subjectivity

4.6.4 Scope and Research Boundary Limitations 
- No assuming accuracy claims
- No lengthy improvement tracking
- No more behavioral performance
